claim: The mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) is a pathological pore in the inner mitochondrial membrane thought to be composed of the F-ATP synthase (complex V).
source: The mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) is a pathological pore in the inner mitochondrial membrane thought to be composed of the F-ATP synthase (complex V).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the scientific literature and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: OSCP, a subunit of F-ATP synthase, helps protect against mPTP formation.
source: OSCP, a subunit of F-ATP synthase, helps protect against mPTP formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the scientific literature.

claim: Loss of OSCP in C. elegans initiates the mPTP and shortens lifespan specifically during adulthood.
source: We have found that loss OSCP in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans initiates the mPTP and shortens lifespan specifically during adulthood, in part via initiation of the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including lifespan assays and mPTP measurements.

claim: Loss of OSCP initiates the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) during adulthood.
source: We have found that loss OSCP in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans initiates the mPTP and shortens lifespan specifically during adulthood, in part via initiation of the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing UPRmt reporter activation.

claim: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of the mPTP inhibits the UPRmt and restores normal lifespan.
source: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of the mPTP inhibits the UPRmt and restores normal lifespan.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using CsA treatment and genetic manipulations.

claim: Loss of the putative pore-forming component of F-ATP synthase extends adult lifespan.
source: Loss of the putative pore-forming component of F-ATP synthase extends adult lifespan, suggesting that the mPTP normally promotes aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mPTP normally promotes aging.
source: Loss of the putative pore-forming component of F-ATP synthase extends adult lifespan, suggesting that the mPTP normally promotes aging.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lifespan extension observed upon loss of the pore-forming component.

claim: The frequency of the mPTP increases with age as mitochondrial function declines.
source: As mitochondrial function declines with age, the frequency of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) increases (Rottenberg and Hoek, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The mPTP is central to early-stage pathologies associated with Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease.
source: The mPTP is central to early-stage pathologies associated with several age-related diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) and late-stage pathologies of ischemia-reperfusion injuries including heart attack and stroke (Ong et al., 2015; Panel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mPTP is central to late-stage pathologies of ischemia-reperfusion injuries including heart attack and stroke.
source: The mPTP is central to early-stage pathologies associated with several age-related diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) and late-stage pathologies of ischemia-reperfusion injuries including heart attack and stroke (Ong et al., 2015; Panel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mPTP is a pathological channel that forms in the inner mitochondrial membrane in response to excessive cytosolic Ca2+ or high ROS conditions.
source: The mPTP is a pathological channel that forms in the inner mitochondrial membrane in response to excessive cytosolic Ca2+ or high ROS conditions.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the mPTP.

claim: Sustained opening of the mPTP leads to outer mitochondrial membrane rupture, release of Ca2+ into the cytosol, and cell death.
source: Sustained opening of the mPTP leads to outer mitochondrial membrane rupture, release of Ca2+ into the cytosol, and cell death (Bernardi and Di Lisa, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cyclosporin A (CsA) inhibits the mPTP by binding and sequestering cyclophilin D.
source: Cyclosporin A (CsA), a well-characterized mPTP inhibitor, inhibits the mPTP by binding and sequestering cyclophilin D, a mitochondrially localized peptidyl prolyl isomerase that helps catalyze pore formation (Basso et al., 2005; Nakagawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cyclophilin D is a mitochondrially localized peptidyl prolyl isomerase that helps catalyze pore formation.
source: Cyclosporin A (CsA), a well-characterized mPTP inhibitor, inhibits the mPTP by binding and sequestering cyclophilin D, a mitochondrially localized peptidyl prolyl isomerase that helps catalyze pore formation (Basso et al., 2005; Nakagawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Genetic inhibition of cyclophilin D protects against mPTP formation.
source: Genetic inhibition of cyclophilin D protects against mPTP formation (Baines et al., 2005), and CsA has been shown to extend lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans (Ye et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CsA has been shown to extend lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Genetic inhibition of cyclophilin D protects against mPTP formation (Baines et al., 2005), and CsA has been shown to extend lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans (Ye et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The mPTP appears to be an important modulator of healthspan and lifespan.
source: Thus, the mPTP appears to be an important modulator of healthspan and lifespan.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the evidence about CsA extending lifespan and cyclophilin D protecting against mPTP.

claim: Many experts in the field of mPTP have pointed to the F-ATP synthase (complex V) as the most probable inner mitochondrial pore candidate.
source: Due to a multitude of recent studies, many experts in the field of mPTP have pointed to the F-ATP synthase (complex V) as the most probable inner mitochondrial pore candidate (Bonora et al., 2017; Carraro et al., 2019; Mnatsakanyan and Jonas, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: F-ATP synthase is able to bind cyclophilin D and form Ca2+ currents.
source: F-ATP synthase is able to bind cyclophilin D and form Ca2+ currents (Bernardi and Di Lisa, 2015; Mnatsakanyan and Jonas, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some models posit that dimeric forms of F-ATP synthase open to form a pore.
source: Some models posit that dimeric forms of F-ATP synthase open to form a pore while other models have suggested that the pore occurs via the membrane-bound proton-driving c-ring rotor (Alavian et al., 2014; Azarashvili et al., 2014; Bonora et al., 2013; Bonora et al., 2017; Giorgio et al., 2013; Mnatsakanyan et al., 2019; Neginskaya et al., 2019; Urbani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Other models have suggested that the pore occurs via the membrane-bound proton-driving c-ring rotor.
source: Some models posit that dimeric forms of F-ATP synthase open to form a pore while other models have suggested that the pore occurs via the membrane-bound proton-driving c-ring rotor (Alavian et al., 2014; Azarashvili et al., 2014; Bonora et al., 2013; Bonora et al., 2017; Giorgio et al., 2013; Mnatsakanyan et al., 2019; Neginskaya et al., 2019; Urbani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Systematic deletion of nearly every subunit of F-ATP synthase in a cell model showed that a pore is still capable of forming.
source: Despite mounting evidence supporting F-ATP synthase as the pore-forming component of the mPTP, systematic deletion of nearly every subunit of F-ATP synthase in a cell model showed that a pore is still capable of forming (Carroll et al., 2019; He et al., 2017a; He et al., 2017b), leading some groups to suggest that in the absence of an intact F-ATP synthase, smaller low-conductance CsA-dependent pores distinct from the mPTP form (Neginskaya et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the absence of an intact F-ATP synthase, smaller low-conductance CsA-dependent pores distinct from the mPTP form.
source: Despite mounting evidence supporting F-ATP synthase as the pore-forming component of the mPTP, systematic deletion of nearly every subunit of F-ATP synthase in a cell model showed that a pore is still capable of forming (Carroll et al., 2019; He et al., 2017a; He et al., 2017b), leading some groups to suggest that in the absence of an intact F-ATP synthase, smaller low-conductance CsA-dependent pores distinct from the mPTP form (Neginskaya et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The mPTP can be mediated by adenine nucleotide transporter (ANT).
source: Other groups have proposed that the mPTP can be mediated by adenine nucleotide transporter (ANT), which exchanges ADP and ATP across the IMM.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Genetic inhibition of ANTs helps prevent pore formation.
source: Genetic inhibition of ANTs helps prevent pore formation (Karch et al., 2019), and the 'multi-pore model' posits that the mPTP can be mediated by ANT, as well as a cyclophilin D binding structure, such as F-ATP synthase, which would explain why deletion of putative pore components may still yield pore formation (Carraro et al., 2019; Karch et al., 2019; Carrer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The 'multi-pore model' posits that the mPTP can be mediated by ANT, as well as a cyclophilin D binding structure, such as F-ATP synthase.
source: Genetic inhibition of ANTs helps prevent pore formation (Karch et al., 2019), and the 'multi-pore model' posits that the mPTP can be mediated by ANT, as well as a cyclophilin D binding structure, such as F-ATP synthase, which would explain why deletion of putative pore components may still yield pore formation (Carraro et al., 2019; Karch et al., 2019; Carrer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: OSCP regulates ATPase rotational activity to provide efficient ATP production.
source: ATP5O, also known as oligomycin sensitivity-conferring protein (OSCP), a subunit of the F-ATP synthase that regulates ATPase rotational activity to provide efficient ATP production (Murphy et al., 2019), has emerged as an important regulator of the mPTP.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: OSCP confers protection against the mPTP under low pH conditions.
source: OSCP confers protection against the mPTP under low pH conditions and loss of OSCP increases propensity for mPTP formation in vitro (Antoniel et al., 2018; Giorgio et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of OSCP increases propensity for mPTP formation in vitro.
source: OSCP confers protection against the mPTP under low pH conditions and loss of OSCP increases propensity for mPTP formation in vitro (Antoniel et al., 2018; Giorgio et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In mice, levels of OSCP decrease with normal aging.
source: In mice, levels of OSCP decrease with normal aging (Gauba et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In mouse models of AD, OSCP binds to amyloid beta (Aβ) and the propensity for mPTP formation increases.
source: In mouse models of AD, OSCP binds to amyloid beta (Aβ) and the propensity for mPTP formation increases, suggesting that the destabilization of OSCP contributes to mPTP formation (Beck et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The destabilization of OSCP contributes to mPTP formation.
source: In mouse models of AD, OSCP binds to amyloid beta (Aβ) and the propensity for mPTP formation increases, suggesting that the destabilization of OSCP contributes to mPTP formation (Beck et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that OSCP binding to Aβ increases mPTP formation.

claim: OSCP overexpression protects from mPTP initiation in AD and cardiac dysfunction models.
source: Conversely, OSCP overexpression protects from mPTP initiation in AD and cardiac dysfunction models (Beck et al., 2016b; Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: OSCP appears to be an important regulator of aging and disease progression, possibly via its ability to modulate mPTP formation.
source: Thus, OSCP appears to be an important regulator of aging and disease progression, possibly via its ability to modulate mPTP formation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the evidence about OSCP's role in mPTP formation and its effects in disease models.

claim: The mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) is capable of initiating a broad-range transcriptional response that aids in the refolding of mitochondrial matrix proteins.
source: Similar to the endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response (UPRER) and the cytoplasmic heat shock response (HSR), the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) is capable of initiating a broad-range transcriptional response that, among other functions, aids in the refolding of mitochondrial matrix proteins (Naresh and Haynes, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) correlates with activation of the UPRmt.
source: Recent studies also show that a loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) correlates with activation of the UPRmt, and disruption of mitochondrial processes other than protein misfolding, such as those involved in TCA cycle and lipid catabolism, also induce the UPRmt (Rolland et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of mitochondrial processes other than protein misfolding, such as those involved in TCA cycle and lipid catabolism, also induce the UPRmt.
source: Recent studies also show that a loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) correlates with activation of the UPRmt, and disruption of mitochondrial processes other than protein misfolding, such as those involved in TCA cycle and lipid catabolism, also induce the UPRmt (Rolland et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: UPRmt activation is associated with longevity and improvement in neurodegenerative models.
source: UPRmt activation is associated with longevity and improvement in neurodegenerative models (Durieux et al., 2011; Houtkooper et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2016; Merkwirth et al., 2016; Sorrentino et al., 2017; Tian et al., 2016), but it has also conversely been shown to increase neurodegeneration, propagate mtDNA mutations, and exacerbate ischemic conditions (Lin et al., 2016; Martinez et al., 2017; Yung et al., 2019), underscoring its complexity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: UPRmt activation has been shown to increase neurodegeneration, propagate mtDNA mutations, and exacerbate ischemic conditions.
source: UPRmt activation is associated with longevity and improvement in neurodegenerative models (Durieux et al., 2011; Houtkooper et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2016; Merkwirth et al., 2016; Sorrentino et al., 2017; Tian et al., 2016), but it has also conversely been shown to increase neurodegeneration, propagate mtDNA mutations, and exacerbate ischemic conditions (Lin et al., 2016; Martinez et al., 2017; Yung et al., 2019), underscoring its complexity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: If left unmitigated, UPRs can initiate cell death.
source: If left unmitigated, UPRs can initiate cell death (Iurlaro and Muñoz-Pinedo, 2016; Münch and Harper, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The context or cellular environment are important determinants of whether UPRmt induction results in beneficial or detrimental effects.
source: Thus, the context or cellular environment are important determinants of whether UPRmt induction results in beneficial or detrimental effects.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the evidence showing both beneficial and detrimental effects of UPRmt activation.

claim: In C. elegans, mild mitochondrial perturbations early in life can extend lifespan.
source: In C. elegans, mild mitochondrial perturbations early in life can extend lifespan.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss of OSCP/atp-3 has previously been shown to extend lifespan when initiated during larval development.
source: Loss of OSCP/atp-3 has previously been shown to extend lifespan when initiated during larval development (Dillin et al., 2002; Rea et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of OSCP/atp-3 during adulthood leads to initiation of the mPTP, the UPRmt, and a shortened lifespan.
source: In contrast, here, we have determined that loss of OSCP/atp-3 during adulthood leads to initiation of the mPTP, the UPRmt, and a shortened lifespan.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: atfs-1, the UPRmt master transcription factor, helps drive the reduction of lifespan.
source: Surprisingly, atfs-1, the UPRmt master transcription factor (Haynes et al., 2010; Nargund et al., 2012), helps drive the reduction of lifespan, suggesting that the UPRmt program can promote aging during adulthood.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that atfs-1 mutants have less lifespan reduction.

claim: The UPRmt program can promote aging during adulthood.
source: Surprisingly, atfs-1, the UPRmt master transcription factor (Haynes et al., 2010; Nargund et al., 2012), helps drive the reduction of lifespan, suggesting that the UPRmt program can promote aging during adulthood.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that atfs-1 helps drive lifespan reduction.

claim: The adult UPRmt is responsive to mPTP regulators, including CsA, a mitochondrially localized cyclophilin, and ANTs.
source: The adult UPRmt is responsive to mPTP regulators, including the immunosuppressive drug, CsA, as well as a mitochondrially localized cyclophilin and ANTs, pointing to a previously undiscovered coordination between the UPRmt and the mPTP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that these factors modulate the UPRmt.

claim: There is a previously undiscovered coordination between the UPRmt and the mPTP.
source: The adult UPRmt is responsive to mPTP regulators, including the immunosuppressive drug, CsA, as well as a mitochondrially localized cyclophilin and ANTs, pointing to a previously undiscovered coordination between the UPRmt and the mPTP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mPTP regulators affect the UPRmt.

claim: The proton-driving rotor subunit and subunits important for dimerization of the F-ATP synthase are essential for transducing the adult UPRmt.
source: We find that the proton-driving rotor subunit as well as subunits important for dimerization of the F-ATP synthase are essential for transducing the adult UPRmt.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that loss of these subunits suppresses the UPRmt.

claim: Loss of the proton-driving rotor subunit and subunits important for dimerization restores lifespan due to loss of OSCP/atp-3.
source: Loss of these subunits as well as pharmacological CsA treatment restores lifespan due to loss of OSCP/atp-3.
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CsA treatment restores lifespan due to loss of OSCP/atp-3.
source: Loss of these subunits as well as pharmacological CsA treatment restores lifespan due to loss of OSCP/atp-3.
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data presented in the manuscript.

claim: These results are consistent with current models that posit that the F-ATP synthase forms the mPTP.
source: These results are consistent with current models that posit that the F-ATP synthase forms the mPTP (Bernardi and Di Lisa, 2015).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Loss of OSCP/atp-3 in adults induces mPTP formation with subsequent activation of the UPRmt.
source: Overall, our findings point to a model in which loss of OSCP/atp-3 in adults induces mPTP formation with subsequent activation of the UPRmt.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A reduction in the abundance of OSCP/atp-3 by RNAi during adulthood caused a loss of MMP.
source: We observed that a reduction in the abundance of OSCP/atp-3 by RNA interference (RNAi) during adulthood caused a loss of MMP as measured by the mitochondrial dye, tetramethylrhodamine methyl ester (TMRM), while RNAi of other OXPHOS subunits from complex I, IV, and V had no effect on the MMP (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: RNAi of other OXPHOS subunits from complex I, IV, and V had no effect on the MMP during adulthood.
source: We observed that a reduction in the abundance of OSCP/atp-3 by RNA interference (RNAi) during adulthood caused a loss of MMP as measured by the mitochondrial dye, tetramethylrhodamine methyl ester (TMRM), while RNAi of other OXPHOS subunits from complex I, IV, and V had no effect on the MMP (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: RNAi of OSCP/atp-3 during adulthood caused an increase in cytosolic Ca2+.
source: RNAi of OSCP/atp-3 during adulthood also caused an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ as measured by the intestinal FRET-based Ca2+ reporter, KWN190, while RNAi of subunits from complex IV and complex V did not (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, E.

claim: RNAi of subunits from complex IV and complex V did not cause an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ during adulthood.
source: RNAi of OSCP/atp-3 during adulthood also caused an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ as measured by the intestinal FRET-based Ca2+ reporter, KWN190, while RNAi of subunits from complex IV and complex V did not (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, E.

claim: CsA rescued the loss of MMP caused by RNAi of OSCP/atp-3 during adulthood.
source: CsA rescued the loss of MMP and suppressed the rise of cytosolic Ca2+ caused by RNAi of OSCP/atp-3 during adulthood (Figure 1C, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, F.

claim: CsA suppressed the rise of cytosolic Ca2+ caused by RNAi of OSCP/atp-3 during adulthood.
source: CsA rescued the loss of MMP and suppressed the rise of cytosolic Ca2+ caused by RNAi of OSCP/atp-3 during adulthood (Figure 1C, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, F.

claim: Loss of OSCP/atp-3 induced mitochondrial swelling and fragmentation compared to control.
source: Loss of OSCP/atp-3 also induced mitochondrial swelling and fragmentation compared to control, which was rescued by CsA (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-J.

claim: CsA rescued the mitochondrial swelling and fragmentation caused by loss of OSCP/atp-3.
source: Loss of OSCP/atp-3 also induced mitochondrial swelling and fragmentation compared to control, which was rescued by CsA (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-J.

claim: FCCP induced a loss of MMP when administered during adulthood.
source: FCCP induced a loss of MMP when administered during adulthood, but did not lead to an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), suggesting that a loss in MMP is not sufficient to recapitulate mPTP characteristics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: FCCP did not lead to an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ when administered during adulthood.
source: FCCP induced a loss of MMP when administered during adulthood, but did not lead to an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), suggesting that a loss in MMP is not sufficient to recapitulate mPTP characteristics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: A loss in MMP is not sufficient to recapitulate mPTP characteristics.
source: FCCP induced a loss of MMP when administered during adulthood, but did not lead to an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), suggesting that a loss in MMP is not sufficient to recapitulate mPTP characteristics.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that FCCP causes MMP loss but not Ca2+ increase.

claim: Loss of OSCP/atp-3 RNAi during development leads to a loss of MMP.
source: Similarly, loss of OSCP/atp-3 RNAi during development, which leads to a loss of MMP, did not lead to an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D), demonstrating that phenotypes that result from a loss of OSCP/atp-3 are distinct during adulthood versus development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Loss of OSCP/atp-3 RNAi during development did not lead to an increase in cytosolic Ca2+.
source: Similarly, loss of OSCP/atp-3 RNAi during development, which leads to a loss of MMP, did not lead to an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D), demonstrating that phenotypes that result from a loss of OSCP/atp-3 are distinct during adulthood versus development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Phenotypes that result from a loss of OSCP/atp-3 are distinct during adulthood versus development.
source: Similarly, loss of OSCP/atp-3 RNAi during development, which leads to a loss of MMP, did not lead to an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D), demonstrating that phenotypes that result from a loss of OSCP/atp-3 are distinct during adulthood versus development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the different effects of OSCP/atp-3 loss during development versus adulthood.

claim: Loss of OSCP/atp-3 during adulthood uniquely induces the mPTP in C. elegans.
source: Overall, these results suggest that loss of OSCP/atp-3 during adulthood uniquely induces the mPTP in C. elegans.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing mPTP characteristics.

claim: RNAi of OSCP/atp-3 selectively induces the UPRmt during adulthood.
source: To determine if RNAi of OSCP/atp-3 selectively induces the UPRmt during adulthood due to its observed loss in MMP (Figure 1A, B), we utilized a GFP reporter under the promoter of the UPRmt chaperone, hsp-6 (phsp-6::GFP) (Yoneda et al., 2004), and compared it to select representative OXPHOS genes encoding complex I, III, IV, and V subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using the phsp-6::GFP reporter.

claim: RNAi of OXPHOS subunits induced little to no UPRmt if initiated after the last larval stage (L4).
source: RNAi of OXPHOS subunits induced little to no UPRmt if initiated after the last larval stage (L4), which we termed the post-developmental UPRmt (pdvUPRmt) (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: RNAi of OSCP/atp-3 induced a robust UPRmt in young adults.
source: The exception was RNAi of OSCP/atp-3, which induced a robust UPRmt in young adults (Figure 2A, B, Figure 2—source data 1), the timing of which corresponded with the loss in MMP (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: The timing of UPRmt induction by OSCP/atp-3 RNAi corresponded with the loss in MMP.
source: The exception was RNAi of OSCP/atp-3, which induced a robust UPRmt in young adults (Figure 2A, B, Figure 2—source data 1), the timing of which corresponded with the loss in MMP (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal correlation between UPRmt induction and MMP loss.

claim: RNAi of all the same genes induced a robust UPRmt if initiated during the early larval stages (L1, L2, and L3) of development.
source: In contrast, RNAi of all the same genes induced a robust UPRmt if initiated during the early larval stages (L1, L2, and L3) of development (dvUPRmt) (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: The UPRmt is robustly induced during development but poorly induced during adulthood in C. elegans.
source: These results are consistent with previous reports demonstrating that the UPRmt is robustly induced during development but poorly induced during adulthood in C. elegans (Durieux et al., 2011; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Treating worms with FCCP during adulthood did not induce the UPRmt.
source: Treating worms with FCCP during adulthood did not induce the UPRmt (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that loss of MMP per se is not sufficient to induce the UPRmt during adulthood.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Loss of MMP per se is not sufficient to induce the UPRmt during adulthood.
source: Treating worms with FCCP during adulthood did not induce the UPRmt (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that loss of MMP per se is not sufficient to induce the UPRmt during adulthood.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that FCCP causes MMP loss but not UPRmt induction.

claim: Post-developmental loss of OSCP/atp-3 increased endogenous transcript levels of hsp-6.
source: Post-developmental loss of OSCP/atp-3 increased endogenous transcript levels of hsp-6 as well as endogenous HSP-6/mtHSP70 protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Post-developmental loss of OSCP/atp-3 increased endogenous HSP-6/mtHSP70 protein levels.
source: Post-developmental loss of OSCP/atp-3 increased endogenous transcript levels of hsp-6 as well as endogenous HSP-6/mtHSP70 protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Post-developmental loss of OSCP/atp-3 mildly induced the mitochondrial chaperone reporter phsp-60::GFP.
source: Post-developmental loss of OSCP/atp-3 mildly induced the mitochondrial chaperone reporter phsp-60::GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Neither the UPRER nor the HSR were induced by post-developmental loss of OSCP/atp-3.
source: Neither the UPRER nor the HSR were induced by post-developmental loss of OSCP/atp-3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: RNAi of clk-1, mrps-5, and tomm-22 did not induce the pdvUPRmt.
source: RNAi of other mitochondrial genes that are known to induce a dvUPRmt, clk-1 (coenzyme Q hydroxylase), mrps-5 (mitochondrial ribosome), and tomm-22 (translocase of outer mitochondrial membrane) (Baker et al., 2012; Bennett et al., 2014; Houtkooper et al., 2013), did not induce the pdvUPRmt (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: The pdvUPRmt was dependent on the master UPRmt transcription factor, atfs-1.

claim: Loss of OSCP destabilizes the remaining F-ATP synthase to increase pore formation.

evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation about OSCP levels and Aβ binding.

source: Thus, our findings support a model in which loss of OSCP/atp-3 induces a conformation change that is favorable for cyclophilin binding to the remaining peripheral stalk proteins or to sites independent of the F-ATP synthase, leading to destabilization of F-ATP synthase, pore formation with a loss of MMP, and subsequent activation of the pdvUPRmt.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on the experimental results and previous literature.

claim: OSCP/atp-3 is prominently accessible in the mitochondrial matrix and has a diverse set of binding partners, such as estradiol and p53.
source: Unlike other F-ATP synthase subunits, OSCP/atp-3 is prominently accessible in the mitochondrial matrix and has a diverse set of binding partners, such as estradiol and p53, which can modulate ATP production (Bergeaud et al., 2013; Zheng and Ramirez, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of OSCP/atp-3 may induce a strong protein misfolding cascade.
source: Its loss may induce a strong protein misfolding cascade, reminiscent of the He and Lemasters mPTP model first proposed in 2002 (He and Lemasters, 2002).
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the characteristics of OSCP/atp-3 and supported by citation to a previous model.

claim: Exposure to oxidants paraquat and manganese have been shown to induce the UPRmt and the mPTP in separate studies.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.
